title: County of Brabant
capsule: The County of Brabant emerged in the 11th century as an imperial fief within the Holy Roman Empire, initially styled the Landgraviate of Brabant, when Emperor Henry IV granted the territory between the Dender and Zenne rivers west of Brussels to Henry III, Count of Louvain, around 1085. The territory grew through inheritance and conquest under the Reginar-Lambert dynasty, combining with the counties of Louvain and Brussels until Emperor Frederick Barbarossa elevated the combined domains to the Duchy of Brabant in 1183, making Duke Henry I one of the most powerful princes in the Low Countries. The county thus served as the core nucleus from which the later wealthy Duchy of Brabant — encompassing present-day Belgian Brabant, the Dutch province of North Brabant, and parts of the Brussels region — ultimately developed.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory is reasonably attested through 11th–12th century imperial charters, but the precise boundaries of the early county are reconstructed from later sources and carry uncertainty.
